edits.find: For macrovascular outcomes: smoking cessation > BP control > statin > glycemic control. If smoking cessation is an option and the patient smokes, it wins — unless the question is scoped to a specific organ ("risk of nephropathy progression" → ACE-I/BP; "microvascular complications" → A1c). Lifestyle answers are traps when vague ("recommend exercise") and winners when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).
edits.with: For macrovascular outcomes: smoking cessation > BP control > statin > glycemic control. In a patient who smokes, smoking cessation ranks first whenever it is offered. The exception is an outcome limited to one organ. For nephropathy progression, choose an ACE-I (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor) or BP control. For microvascular complications, choose A1c control. Lifestyle advice is the wrong choice when vague ("recommend exercise") and the right choice when specific and high-magnitude (smoking or alcohol cessation).

edits.find: Petechiae with a count of 8,000 in a healthy young woman → ITP → steroids/IVIG, not transfusion (transfused platelets get consumed too) · heparin day 5–10 with a 50% drop → HIT → stop heparin, start argatroban, never transfuse · clumps on the smear → pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA → repeat in a citrate tube — the one time "recheck the count" is correct · DDAVP is for qualitative defects (von Willebrand disease, mild hemophilia A, uremic platelet dysfunction), not for a low count.
edits.with: Petechiae with a count of 8,000 in a healthy young woman indicate ITP (immune thrombocytopenia) → steroids or IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin), not transfusion. Transfused platelets are consumed too · a 50% drop on heparin day 5–10 indicates HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) → stop heparin, start argatroban and never transfuse · clumps on the smear indicate pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) → repeat in a citrate tube. This is the one time "recheck the count" is correct · DDAVP (desmopressin) is for qualitative defects (von Willebrand disease, mild hemophilia A, uremic platelet dysfunction), not for a low count.

edits.find: The stem's deciding words are "unprocessed" and "no supplements." A well-planned vegan diet meets most needs — the exam's fork is which nutrients cannot come from unfortified plants: B12 always, vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only ~half the requirement, less in northern latitudes), and calcium (plant sources are oxalate-bound). Iron and zinc join the list for children and menstruating women. The planted wrong answers are folate and protein — abundant in legumes, greens, and grains.
edits.with: A well-planned vegan diet meets most needs. This patient eats an "unprocessed" vegan diet and takes "no supplements." Nutrients that cannot come from unfortified plants: B12 always · vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only ~half the requirement, less in northern latitudes) · calcium (plant sources are oxalate-bound). For children and menstruating women, add iron and zinc. Legumes, greens and grains are rich in folate and protein, so neither needs supplementing.
